current_activity: assaulting Juno and Sword beaches
notes: Assault corps (Crocker) at Juno and Sword plus Orne airborne flank; Caen not taken on D-Day and I Corps linked with XXX Corps by end of D-Day.

current_activity: delayed 51st Highland Division attack from the Orne bridgehead, contained by 21st Panzer; bridgehead also under attack
notes: I Corps' planned eastern thrust (51st (Highland) Division and 4th Armoured Brigade crossing into the 6th Airborne Division's Orne bridgehead, toward Cagny south-east of Caen) was postponed to 12 June because bad weather delayed the landing of the 51st Division and 4th Armoured Brigade (Wikipedia, Operation Perch, citing Ellis). The corps' own attack on 12 June was limited: the bridgehead was itself attacked all day from the Bréville area (346th Infantry Division per the Battle of Bréville page; the 21st Panzer Division was also opposing from the south), the Germans pulled back in the evening, and 12th Parachute Battalion and a Devonshire company captured Bréville that night. The 51st Division, opposed by 21st Panzer in its push south toward Sainte-Honorine, was contained, and the offensive east of Caen was called off on 13 June. The fighting was done by divisions (51st Highland, 6th Airborne), not by the corps headquarters; the point is a representative bridgehead point (Bréville-les-Monts commune coordinates), not the corps HQ. current_activity: Passes from Second Army to First Canadian Army at noon; Stacey calls it 1st British Corps
notes: Event date: 23 July 1944, noon (Stacey, p. 196). Event definition: The corps front east of the Orne passes from Second Army to the headquarters of First Canadian Army, which becomes operational at noon; the corps stays under the Army until March 1945 (p. 198). This is the only claim of I Corps in Canadian Batch 1: a minimal record kept as evidence for the command relations, not a unit claim set (the British batch comes later). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 196: "at noon on 23 July Headquarters First Canadian Army became operational, though as yet it had no Canadian divisions under its command. It took over at that moment the front held by Lieut.-General J. T. Crocker's 1st British Corps"; p. 198: "the 1st British Corps operated under the First Canadian Army through the weeks and months that followed". Location: Orne bridgehead / east of Caen (existing area place PL0265) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the existing area place east of Caen and stands for the corps front; it is not a headquarters position. Location support: Stacey (p. 196) gives the corps front only as the area between the Caen-Mezidon railway and the Channel, with no town. Commander: Lt.-Gen. J. T. Crocker.

current_activity: Le Havre falls: Fort de Tourneville surrenders in the morning, Fort St. Addresse at 15:30; over 11,300 prisoners
notes: Event date: 12 September 1944 (Ellis, vol. II, p. 15). Event definition: The battle for Le Havre is resumed on 12 September: Fort de Tourneville surrenders during the morning, the wounded garrison commander giving himself up, and Fort St. Addresse at about 15:30; over 11,300 prisoners are taken for under 500 casualties; the harbour is so thoroughly demolished that shipping cannot use the port until 9 October (p. 15). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 15: "Fort de Tourneville surrendered during the morning"; "Fort St. Addresse surrendered at about 3.30 p.m. and when all mopping up was completed over 11,300 prisoners had been taken". Location: Le Havre, France (existing place PL0169) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is the town of Le Havre, where the forts surrendered; the corps headquarters is not named. Location support: Ellis names Le Havre and the two forts (p. 15); the corps headquarters is not named. Commander: Lt.-Gen. J. T. Crocker (Ellis, vol. I, p. 170 names him as the I Corps commander at the landings and p. 432 as the corps commander in August). Review (British Batch 2, 28 October 2026; inferred value; old value: operation_id OP-CAMP-NORTHERN-FRANCE; new value: operation_id OP-ASTONIA): the row is part of the I Corps assault on Le Havre of 10 to 12 September 1944, which Stacey, p. 331, calls a neat and expeditious three-day operation in the second week of September and names Operation Astonia; the new operation is a child of OP-CAMP-NORTHERN-FRANCE, so the narrower operation replaces the broader one. The other rows under OP-CAMP-NORTHERN-FRANCE are not about Le Havre.
